title: The ternary (conditional) operator ?:

visuals.title: Nested ternary grade: marks >= 80 ? A : marks >= 65 ? B : marks >= 50 ? C : F

goal: After this you can use the ?: operator to choose between two values in one line, put it safely inside cout, and decide when a normal if-else is the better choice.
warmup: At the canteen the cashier thinks: 'If the student has a card, the price is 100, otherwise the price is 120.' One question, two possible answers, and you simply pick one. Programs do this all the time: if marks are 50 or more the result is Pass, otherwise Fail. The ternary operator lets you write this pick in one short line.
definition: The ternary operator ?: is a short if-else that produces a value. It is called ternary because it has three parts: a condition, a value for true, and a value for false. It is written condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse. If the condition is true you get the first value, otherwise the second.
howItWorks: The computer checks the condition first. If it is true, only the value after the ? is used. If it is false, only the value after the : is used. The other one is ignored. Because the whole thing is a value, you can store it in a variable or print it. When you print it inside cout, always put the whole ternary in brackets, because << has higher priority than ?: and would otherwise grab only a piece of it.
syntax:
// condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse
int larger = (a > b) ? a : b;                          // store the chosen value
cout << ((marks >= 50) ? "Pass" : "Fail");               // print it: use outer brackets
string g = (m >= 80) ? "A" : (m >= 50) ? "B" : "F";    // nesting: keep it short

worked.problem: Read a number. Print whether it is even or odd, and print the smaller of the number and 10. Use ternary operators inside cout.

IF number < 10 THEN pick number ELSE pick 10

sample.title: Even or odd, and min with 10
sample.expectedOutput:
Enter a number: 7 is odd
Smaller of number and 10 is 7

explanation.text: The whole ternary is inside its own brackets. number % 2 == 0 is the condition. It picks the word even or odd.
Another ternary inside cout. It picks number if number < 10, otherwise 10, so the smaller value is printed.

steps.note: The user types 7, so number is 7.
7 % 2 is 1, so number % 2 == 0 is false. The ternary picks the value after the colon: odd.
7 < 10 is true, so the ternary picks the value after the question mark: number, which is 7.

worked.problem: Read marks and print the grade: A for 80 or more, B for 65 or more, C for 50 or more, otherwise F. Use a nested ternary operator.
pseudocode: ELSE IF marks >= 65 THEN grade = B
ELSE IF marks >= 50 THEN grade = C

sample.title: Grade with a nested ternary

explanation.text: string lets us store words such as A or B.

Read it left to right: if marks >= 80 the answer is A, otherwise ask the next question. The nested part is the false-branch of the first ?:. With 72 the first test fails, the second (>= 65) is true, so grade is B.
Prints the grade. Two nesting levels is already hard to read, so for more cases an else-if ladder is better.

variations.when: Print one of two values (outer brackets needed)
Each side can be an expression
Three or more outcomes (keep to two levels at most)
Several statements, or a clearer layout

mistakes.error: no match for 'operator>' (operand types are 'std::basic_ostream<char>' and 'int')
expected ':' before ';' token (the ternary needs both the true value and the false value)
no match for 'operator>=' (operand types are 'std::basic_ostream<char>' and 'int')
No compiler error, but deep nesting is very hard to read and easy to get wrong. Use else-if instead.

examTips: Syntax to memorise: condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse; It has three parts, so it is called ternary.
It is an expression: it gives a value, so you can assign it or print it. An if-else is a statement and does not give a value.
Inside cout, put the whole ternary in brackets: cout << (a > b ? a : b);
Both sides of the colon should have the same kind of value (both numbers, or both text).
Use it for short two-way choices. For many cases or several statements, use if-else.
romanSummary: Ternary operator ?: chhota sa if-else hai jo ek value deta hai.
Misal: larger = (a > b) ? a : b; yani a bara ho to a, warna b.
cout ke andar use karte waqt poora ternary brackets mein likhein.
Sirf chhote aur simple faislon ke liye use karein; lambi logic ke liye normal if-else behtar hai.

practice.prompt: How many parts (operands) does the ternary operator have?
practice.hint: Condition, value if true, value if false.
practice.explanation: Ternary means three: the condition and two values.
8 > 12 is false, so the value after the colon (b = 12) is printed.

practice.hint: The first test fails, so go to the nested ternary.
practice.explanation: n > 0 is false, so we evaluate (n < 0) ? -1 : 0. n < 0 is true, so r becomes -1.

practice.explanation: p > 3 is false, so p + 1 is used: 2 + 1 = 3.

practice.prompt:
Fix the bug so it prints the bigger number:

cout << "Bigger: " << a > b ? a : b << endl;
practice.explanation: Without brackets, cout << "Bigger: " << a is compared with b. Brackets keep the ternary together.

practice.prompt: Write a program that reads an integer and prints, for example, '10 is even' or '7 is odd', using a ternary operator inside cout.
practice.explanation: An even number has no remainder when divided by 2.

practice.prompt: Write a program that reads three integers and prints the smallest one using ternary operators only (no if).
practice.hint: Compare a and b first, then compare the winner with c.
practice.explanation: If a < b, the smaller of a and c is the answer; otherwise the smaller of b and c.

quiz.prompt: What is the correct syntax of the ternary operator?
quiz.explanation: The condition comes first, then ?, the true value, :, and the false value.
The condition is true, so the first value is chosen.

quiz.prompt: Which line prints Pass or Fail correctly?
quiz.hint: The whole ternary needs brackets inside cout.
quiz.explanation: Brackets stop << from grabbing part of the expression.

quiz.prompt: When is a normal if-else better than the ternary operator?
options: When picking one of two simple values
When each choice needs several statements
When you want shorter code at any cost
quiz.answer: When each choice needs several statements
quiz.explanation: The ternary is for short two-way value choices. Several statements or many cases are clearer in if-else.

quiz.prompt: int x = 7; What does cout << (x % 2 == 0 ? 1 : 2); print?
quiz.explanation: x % 2 == 0 is false, so the value after the colon (2) is printed.
